974.title: A good apology
974.hook: a study by Roy Lewicki and colleagues found the most important parts are owning responsibility and offering repair
974.howItsDone: Researchers who study apologies, including Roy Lewicki and colleagues, describe an effective apology as one that clearly acknowledges responsibility and offers to repair the harm; in Matthew 5, reconciliation comes before offering a gift at the altar.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was restorative justice: who was hurt, what do they need, and Zacchaeus offering to restore fourfold. Your line was repair. Now the other side of the table: the one who did the harm.

"I'm sorry if anyone was offended." It has the word sorry right there in it, and still it can land like a door clicking shut. So can its cousins: sorry you feel that way, mistakes were made, I said I was sorry, what more do you want? Each one is an apology that somehow isn't one. A team of researchers led by Roy Lewicki took apologies apart, piece by piece, to find out which pieces actually do the work.
screen: `SORRY IF ANYONE WAS OFFENDED.` → `AN APOLOGY THAT ISN'T ONE.` → `TAKING APOLOGIES APART.`

segments.voice: Lewicki and his colleagues listed the parts an apology can have: saying you regret it, explaining what went wrong, acknowledging that you're responsible, saying you've changed, offering to repair the damage, and asking to be forgiven. Then they asked people to judge apologies built from different mixes of those parts. The piece that mattered most was acknowledging responsibility. Next came offering repair. And the piece that mattered least was asking for forgiveness. The apology works best when it's about what the speaker did and will do, and least when it asks something of the person who was hurt. Look at the door-clicking apology again. "If anyone was offended" doesn't own anything. Its subject is the other person's feelings, not the speaker's action. Owning sounds like a sentence with I at the front: I did this, and it was wrong. Repair answers the next question: and here's what I'll do about it. An older text sets the same order, and makes it urgent. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus describes someone bringing a gift to the altar who remembers there that a brother has something against him: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." The repair comes before the worship. The text doesn't wait for the brother to come asking; the one at the altar gets up and goes. And the gift waits there until he's back.
screen: `THE PARTS OF AN APOLOGY.` · `OWNING IT MATTERED MOST.` · `IF ANYONE WAS OFFENDED OWNS NOTHING.` · `FIRST BE RECONCILED.` · then, large: `OWN IT, REPAIR IT.`

segments.voice: Choose one person you owe an apology to, small or large, and build it in your head from just two parts: own it, starting with I, I did this and it was wrong; then repair, here's what I'll do. Notice any urge to add a but, an if, or an explanation, leave it off, and say the two sentences once more, slowly, as if they were listening.
Lewicki. The researcher whose study found owning responsibility and offering repair mattered most in an apology. Today's word.
Your line: own it, repair it. No if, no but. Day nine hundred seventy-four, done.

975.title: Forgiveness and health
975.hook: studies link forgiving with lower stress, though cause and effect are unclear
975.howItsDone: Researchers study forgiveness and health with questionnaires and body measures such as heart rate and blood pressure; they report links between forgiving and lower stress while saying cause and effect are not settled.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Lewicki: own it, starting with I, then offer repair. Your line was own it, repair it.

A line from the book of Proverbs: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones." Whoever wrote it had a hunch that what happens in the heart shows up in the body, down to the bones. Researchers now test hunches like that with questionnaires, heart monitors and blood pressure readings, and some of them have pointed those tools at forgiveness. What they found is worth hearing. So is what they're careful not to claim.
screen: `A MERRY HEART, LIKE A MEDICINE.` → `A HUNCH ABOUT HEART AND BODY.` → `RESEARCHERS TEST IT.`

segments.voice: In the research gathered in the book Forgiveness and Health, edited by Loren Toussaint, Everett Worthington and David Williams, people who forgive more readily tend to report less stress. Forgiving and lower stress show up together. Now the honest catch, and it's a big one. Showing up together is not the same as one causing the other. Maybe forgiving lowers stress. Maybe people who are already less stressed find it easier to forgive. Maybe something else, like good sleep or good friends, helps both at once. The researchers themselves say the direction isn't settled, and anyone who promises that forgiving will fix your blood pressure is saying more than the studies do. A closer look at one moment: the psychologist Charlotte Witvliet asked people to bring to mind someone who had hurt them, and then to spend time either rehearsing the grudge or imagining forgiving. While they rehearsed the grudge, their bodies showed more signs of stress: heart rate and blood pressure went up. While they imagined forgiving, those signs were lower. That's a small window, measured in minutes, not a lifetime. But it shows a grudge isn't only a thought. The body takes part. So what do you do with a link you can't fully explain? Not treat forgiveness like a pill. Treat it as something to notice: what holding does in your own shoulders, and what letting go does. The Proverbs writer never ran a study. The hunch was about bones.

segments.voice: Hold one small grievance, nothing heavy, for a few breaths, and check in with the body: the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, the breath itself. Then try letting it go, even only for the length of this sit, and check in again; there's no right result, and whatever you find, or don't, is worth knowing.
Witvliet. The psychologist whose study found the body's stress signs rose during a rehearsed grudge, and fell while imagining forgiving. Today's word.
Your line: lighter. Not a cure, just something worth noticing in your own body. See you tomorrow.

976.title: Small things first
976.hook: practice on small grievances before big ones
976.howItsDone: Some forgiveness programs suggest practicing first on minor, everyday grievances, such as a rude remark or a late friend, before working on deeper hurts.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Witvliet: forgiving and lower stress show up together, though which causes which is still unclear. Your line was lighter. Today the theme turns from the research to practices.

At the end of a rack of weights in a gym sits the lightest one, small enough to lift with two fingers. It's there on purpose: muscles learn the movement on it before they're asked to carry anything heavy. Forgiveness tends to get talked about at the heavy end of the rack: betrayal, cruelty, the things that change a life. Those are real, and they matter. But the movement itself, noticing a hurt and letting it go, can be learned on something much lighter. Today starts at the other end of the rack.
screen: `THE LIGHTEST WEIGHT IN THE RACK.` → `FORGIVENESS AT THE HEAVY END.` → `START AT THE OTHER END.`

segments.voice: The Tao Te Ching, in its sixty-third chapter, says that the difficult things of the world are done while they are still easy, and the great things of the world while they are still small. In Chinese, the word for small there is xi: small, fine, slender. The great begins in the small. A line from Luke's Gospel says something close: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." The least comes first, and it isn't wasted practice. It's where the habit forms. And the small things are everywhere. The person who took the last coffee. The friend who was late again. The roommate who left the dishes. The comment in the group chat that stung a little. Grievances this size come along all day, so the practice can too, several times before lunch. Each one is a chance to run the whole motion in miniature: notice it, name it plainly, and let it go. A motion done often becomes familiar. When something heavy does come, the movement of letting go isn't brand new; it has been rehearsed on small things, again and again. Starting small isn't a way of pretending the big wounds don't exist. And it doesn't put them on a schedule. Not yet is still allowed for those. It just means the first rep happens on the lightest weight in the rack.
screen: `THE GREAT BEGINS IN THE SMALL.` · `FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.` · `SMALL GRIEVANCES ARE EVERYWHERE.` · `THE SAME MOTION, REHEARSED.` · then, large: `START SMALL.`

segments.voice: Find one small grievance from the last day or two, the smaller the better, a door not held, a slow checkout, and name it plainly in one sentence. Then set it down the way you'd set down the lightest weight, without ceremony, and if another small one comes up, do the same: notice, name, release.
Xi. The Chinese word for small, fine, slender, from the Tao Te Ching's teaching that great things begin small. Today's word.
Your line: start small. The heavy end of the rack can wait. That's day nine hundred seventy-six.

977.title: Forgiving yourself
977.hook: the sources that speak of being forgiven also leave room to forgive yourself
977.howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness practice as the Visuddhimagga describes it, the meditator first wishes themselves well and then extends the wish to others; Jewish and Christian readers often turn to Psalm 103 when speaking about being forgiven.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was xi, small: great things begin while they're still small. Your line was start small. Today, the person at the back of the line, the one some people find hardest to forgive.

The meeting was three weeks ago. Dana said the sharp thing, the room went quiet, and she apologized first thing the next morning. Her coworker waved it off: honestly, it's fine, already forgotten. And still, in the shower, at a red light, at two in the morning, the scene plays again, with Dana cast as the villain. She has forgiven people for much worse. The one she can't seem to reach is herself. The old texts have a few things to say about that last person in line. Today: forgiving yourself.
screen: `THE SCENE PLAYS AGAIN.` → `THEY LET IT GO.` → `THE LAST PERSON IN LINE.`

segments.voice: First, the Psalms. Psalm 103 says how far forgiveness carries a wrong away: "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." East and west never meet. In the psalm, a forgiven wrong isn't kept on a shelf, to be taken down again at two in the morning. Second, the Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, in Max Müller's translation: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." It doesn't say the deeds never happened. The clouds were real. But the moon is not the clouds. Buddhist tradition connects this verse with Angulimala, a man remembered for terrible violence who became a monk. Third, where you stand in the circle. The Visuddhimagga, a classic Buddhist manual, teaches loving-kindness by starting with yourself: wish yourself well first, as the example, then widen the same wish to others. You know from the inside how much you want to be happy, so you can wish it for everyone else. When kindness goes around the room: me too. Fourth, this isn't pretending. The psalm still says transgressions; the verse still says evil deeds. In this lesson, forgiving yourself comes after the owning: after the apology, after repairing what you can. What's left is the replay that no longer teaches you anything. Keep the lesson, put down the punishment.
screen: `AS FAR AS THE EAST IS FROM THE WEST.` · `THE MOON IS NOT THE CLOUDS.` · `LOVING-KINDNESS STARTS WITH YOU.` · `KEEP THE LESSON, DROP THE PUNISHMENT.` · then, large: `ME TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you did that still replays, a sharp word or a promise you let slide, and look at it plainly: yes, that happened, and if something's left to repair, note it for later. Then place yourself inside the kindness you'd offer a friend who told you this story, and say the Visuddhimagga's simple wish quietly: may I be happy. If you pray, you can bring this to God in your own way.
Forgiving yourself. Owning what you did, then letting yourself into the same circle of kindness you offer others. Today's word.
Your line: me too. You belong inside your own kindness as much as anyone. Day nine hundred seventy-seven, done.

978.title: Asking forgiveness
978.howItsDone: Some Jewish families ask one another for forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur, and Christians often read the prodigal son in Luke 15 as a picture of coming home to ask forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving yourself. Your line was me too: you belong in your own circle of kindness. Today, the other person.

A man stands on a doorstep with his hand raised to knock. On the drive over he rehearsed three versions, each a little shorter. His heart is going faster than it did at his job interview. Inside is a friend he hasn't spoken to since the night he said the thing. Nothing is stopping him from knocking, except that once he does, the next part isn't up to him. Forgiving happens inside you. Asking puts it in somebody else's hands. Today: asking forgiveness.
screen: `A HAND RAISED TO KNOCK.` → `THREE REHEARSED VERSIONS.` → `THE NEXT PART ISN'T UP TO HIM.`

segments.voice: First, who has to ask. The Mishnah, in its tractate on Yom Kippur, teaches that the Day of Atonement covers wrongs between a person and God, but wrongs between people aren't covered until you make peace with the person you wronged. The holiest day can't do the asking for you, and neither can a prayer said alone or a good intention kept to yourself. Some Jewish families keep a custom of asking one another's forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur for exactly this reason. Second, the rehearsal. In Luke's story of the prodigal son, the younger son, broke and hungry, plans his speech on the way home: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee." He even plans to ask to be taken on as a hired servant. That's the man at the door with three versions. Third, what happens. Luke says: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." The son starts his speech, and the father cuts it short with a robe and a ring. The hired-servant line never gets said. The courage was in the walking home; the speech mattered less than he thought. Fourth, what asking can't control. Not every door opens like that one. The other person may say no, or not yet. That's why it takes nerve: you walk up the path without knowing the answer, and say the two plain words.
screen: `THE HOLY DAY CAN'T ASK FOR YOU.` · `A SPEECH REHEARSED ON THE ROAD.` · `HIS FATHER SAW HIM, AND RAN.` · `THE ANSWER ISN'T YOURS TO CONTROL.` · then, large: `I'M SORRY.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind whom you'd like to ask for forgiveness, someone safe to approach, for something you can honestly own. Notice what your body does at the thought, the tight chest, the urge to explain, and find a first sentence that's short and has no excuses in it. Asking forgiveness. Owning a wrong to the person you wronged, and leaving their answer in their hands. Today's word.
Your line: I'm sorry. Two plain words, with no "but" after them. See you tomorrow.

979.title: Making amends
979.hook: repair where you can, without causing more harm
979.howItsDone: In Alcoholics Anonymous, members work through making amends to people they've harmed, often with a sponsor's help in deciding when direct contact would cause harm; some readers of Numbers 5 take its pattern, confession first and then repayment to the person wronged, as a model for amends today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asking forgiveness: owning a wrong and leaving the answer in the other person's hands. Your line was I'm sorry. Today, what comes after the words.

A borrowed drill comes back with a cracked case. The borrower says sorry, means it, and hands it over. The owner says no problem. And the drill is still cracked. Words can mend a lot between two people. They can't mend a drill. Between I'm sorry and the end of the matter there's a second step, older than any apology study: putting back what you can. An old law in the book of Numbers spells it out, down to a fraction. Today: making amends.
screen: `THE DRILL IS STILL CRACKED.` → `WORDS CAN'T MEND IT.` → `PUT BACK WHAT YOU CAN.`

segments.voice: First, the law. Numbers, chapter five, describes someone who has wronged another person: "Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed." Confession comes first, but the words don't close the matter. Then the principal, the thing itself, put back, and a fifth on top. Second, where it goes: to the one wronged. Not a general donation, not a vague promise to be better. The repair has a name and an address. Third, the limit. Alcoholics Anonymous, in its Big Book, describes making direct amends to the people one has harmed, wherever possible, except when doing so would injure them or others. Sometimes contacting someone would reopen a wound they've worked hard to close. Repair that causes fresh harm isn't repair. Fourth, when you can't go back. The next verse in Numbers imagines a wronged man with no kinsman left to receive the repayment, and it still gets paid, to the Lord, through the priest. The debt finds another place to go. Some people today make what's sometimes called a living amend: changing the behavior for good, or doing for someone else what they owed the person they can't reach. Making it right isn't always making it undone. It's the most honest repair the situation allows.
screen: `CONFESS, THEN PUT IT BACK, PLUS A FIFTH.` · `TO THE ONE YOU WRONGED.` · `EXCEPT WHEN IT WOULD HARM.` · `NO ONE TO RECEIVE IT? IT STILL GOES.` · then, large: `MAKE IT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you owe someone, not a feeling but a thing: a borrowed book, a broken promise, a credit you took, a loan, an hour of help. Ask slowly what would put it back, and whether doing that would hurt them or anyone else. If the road is open, choose one concrete step; if it's closed, picture who could receive a living amend in their place.
Making amends. Putting back what you can, specifically, without causing fresh harm along the way. Today's word.
Your line: make it right. Sorry is the words; amends are the thing put back. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine.

980.title: The unsent letter
980.hook: write it all, then don't send it
980.howItsDone: Some counselors and grief groups suggest writing a letter to a person who hurt you, or who has died, and keeping it rather than sending it; Jews and Christians who pray the psalms often describe them as a place to pour out what can't be said elsewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, making amends: sorry is the words, amends put the thing back. Your line was make it right. Today, the opposite move: something you write and never deliver.

There's a message sitting in a drafts folder. It's been there for months. It's long, unfair in places and exactly right in others. It says everything that never got said at the funeral, or in the breakup, or at the last family dinner. Every so often its writer opens it, adds a line, and closes it again. It has never been sent, and that may be the wisest thing about it. Today: the unsent letter.
screen: `A MESSAGE IN THE DRAFTS FOLDER.` → `UNFAIR IN PLACES, RIGHT IN OTHERS.` → `NEVER SENT.`

segments.voice: First, the old permission to pour it all out. Psalm 62 says: "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him." Pour, not a measured spoonful, not the polite version. The psalms hold a great deal of speech that goes up and gets no reply on the page: grief, rage, pleading, thanks. The letter is a little like that. It gets to be whole. Second, the quieter half. Psalm 4 says: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." Talk it through with yourself, then stop. An unsent letter does both: you write until there's nothing left to say, then put the pen down. Third, why not send it. Yesterday's limit applies: repair that would injure someone isn't repair, and a letter written in full heat often would. The unsent letter keeps the honesty and drops the damage. Some counselors suggest it for that reason, and for the dead, the unreachable, or the person it isn't safe to contact. Fourth, what to do with it. Keep it in a drawer and read it in a month, noticing what's changed. Some people burn it or tear it up as a small ending. The point isn't the paper. The words left your head and went somewhere, so you don't have to keep rehearsing them in the car.
screen: `POUR OUT YOUR HEART.` · `COMMUNE WITH YOUR HEART, BE STILL.` · `HONESTY WITHOUT THE DAMAGE.` · `IN A DRAWER, OR IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `SAID, NOT SENT.`

segments.voice: With a pen, or a blank note on your phone with no recipient, write one person's name at the top, then write fast, without fixing anything: what happened, what it cost you, what you wish they knew. Don't be fair or polite; nobody will read it. When it's emptied out, add one last line, I've said it, and put the page somewhere safe. If you pray, you can offer it up, poured out, as the psalm says.
Drafts folder. Where an honest letter can sit, written all the way down to someone, and never delivered. Today's word.
Your line: said, not sent. That closes the week, from a good apology to a letter you keep. Day nine hundred eighty, done.
